title: 道德經 第四十四章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 44, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 74. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 44 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 立戒 (Setting Up a Warning). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

morph.gloss: a name; one's name in the world, reputation
yǔ: and, together with — joining two nouns for comparison
the body; and so one's own person, oneself
close, near of kin; dear to one

sentences.l: Name and body — which is nearer to you?
sentences.i: Your name or your own person: which is closer to you?
sentences.n:
Three questions open the chapter and none of them has a verb 'to be'. Two nouns, 與 to yoke them, 孰 to ask which, and an adjective — that is the whole sentence, and English has to add a copula to make it stand.

孰 asks 'which of these', not 'who' in general; you have met it in chapters 15 and 23. 親 is the word for blood relations — 六親, the six degrees of kindred, in chapter 18 — so the question is literally which of the two is your kin. Your reputation is not.

身 is a thread running through the book: chapter 13's 貴大患若身 and 吾所以有大患者，為吾有身, and chapter 7's sage who puts his own person last and finds it comes first. It means the body and it means the self, and the book never separates them.

morph.gloss: goods, commodities, valuables — things worth having and hoarding
the more, the greater — here of worth, not of number

sentences.l: Body and goods — which is the more?
sentences.i: Your own person or your goods: which counts for more?
sentences.n: 多 ordinarily means 'many'. Here it is comparative and about weight rather than count — which of the two amounts to more. 貨 was already flagged in chapter 3 (不貴難得之貨, do not prize goods that are hard to come by) and chapter 12; it is always the wrong kind of having.

morph.gloss: getting, gain — the verb used as a noun
losing, loss — to have a thing perish or go
an illness, what ails you; and so harm, the thing that does the damage

sentences.l: Getting and losing — which is the sickness?
sentences.i: Gaining or losing: which is the affliction?
sentences.n:
The third question is the one the first two were built to make possible. Ask whether name or self is dearer and the answer is easy; ask whether gaining or losing is the disease and the obvious answer is losing. The chapter does not answer the question; the two lines that follow simply put the cost on the side of the getting, and leave the reader to draw it. Wang Bi's comment does the same, restating the question rather than settling it: to gain much profit and lose your own person — which of the two is the ailment?

得 and 亡 are verbs pressed into service as nouns, with nothing to mark it. 病 is a physical word, an actual illness, and using it of a moral condition is as much a figure in Chinese as in English.

sentences.t:
是故甚愛必大費，
多藏必厚亡，

morph.gloss: for this reason, therefore — a fused connective, like 是以
excessively, to the point of too much
to be fond of, to set one's heart on; also to be sparing of, to grudge
to spend, to lay out; expense, waste
cáng: to store up, to lay by, to hoard
to lose, to have a thing perish

sentences.l:
For this reason: to be over-fond is bound to cost dearly,
to hoard much is bound to lose heavily.
sentences.i: And so: set your heart on a thing and it will cost you dear; store up much and you will lose much.
sentences.n:
是故 is a fused connective, 'for this reason' — the same kind of unit as 是以, which the book uses some thirty-odd times, and it is one tap because neither half gives you 'therefore' on its own. As a connective it appears only here; chapter 22's 不自是故彰 sets the two characters side by side, but there they belong to different words.

必 does what English 'must' does in 'that must cost you': not a command but an inference about what cannot fail to follow.

愛 is a wide word — to love, to cherish, and also to be close-fisted about. 甚愛 is the attachment that will not let a thing circulate, and Wang Bi reads it that way: what is loved too much is not let out among things, and what is hoarded is not shared out, so the more you gather the more there is to come after, and the cost and the loss follow from the gathering itself. The point is not that misers are punished. It is arithmetic — you cannot lose what you never held.

sentences.t:
知足不辱，
知止不殆，
可以長久。

morph.gloss: to be disgraced, to be put to shame
to stop; where to stop, the place to halt
to come to harm, to be brought into danger
cháng: long, for a long time

sentences.l:
Know enough and you are not disgraced,
know where to stop and you come to no harm,
and so you can last long.
sentences.i: Know what is enough and no disgrace touches you; know where to stop and no harm comes; and so you may last a long time.
sentences.n:
知足 and 知止 are both fixed phrases of this book and both have been met: 知足者富, the one who knows enough is rich (chapter 33), and 知止所以不殆, knowing where to stop is what keeps you from harm (chapter 32). The second of those is almost word for word the middle line here. Repetition on this scale is normal in the Daodejing and is one of the reasons it is thought to have grown out of circulating sayings rather than to have been written straight through.

可以 is two words, not the single 'can' it has become in modern Chinese: 可 'may' and 以 'thereby'. The 以 has lost its object again, as it does all through the book — thereby, that is, by knowing enough and knowing where to stop.

殆 dài and 久 jiǔ belonged to one Old Chinese rhyme group and closed these lines on a chime that Mandarin has lost entirely. Nothing in the modern reading tells you the chapter ends in rhyme.
